description: Active and Passive Voice question bank derived from FDA & SDA Competitive Examination Notes. Covers voice concepts, transitivity, tense-wise conversion, modals, negatives, interrogatives, imperatives, two-object verbs, special structures, non-passive verbs, common errors, and practice questions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is voice in English grammar?

options.A: The grammatical form of a verb that shows whether the subject performs or receives an action
options.B: The tense of a verb showing time of action
options.C: The number of the subject in a sentence
options.D: The mood of a verb expressing command

questions.explanation: Voice is the grammatical form of a verb that shows whether the subject performs an action or receives the action.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the two voices in English?
questions.explanation: The two voices in English are active voice and passive voice.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is active voice?

options.A: The subject receives the action of the verb
options.B: The subject performs the action of the verb

questions.explanation: A sentence is in the active voice when its subject performs the action, e.g., 'The police arrested the thief.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is passive voice?

options.A: The subject performs the action of the verb
options.B: The subject receives or is affected by the action

questions.explanation: A sentence is in the passive voice when its subject receives or is affected by the action, e.g., 'The thief was arrested by the police.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the basic active voice structure?
questions.explanation: The basic active voice structure is Subject + Verb + Object, e.g., 'The child broke the window.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the basic passive voice structure?

options.B: Object of active + suitable form of be + past participle (V3) + by + subject of active

questions.explanation: Passive structure: Object of active sentence + suitable form of be + past participle (V3) + by + subject of active sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to the object in passive voice?

options.B: It becomes the subject of the passive sentence

questions.explanation: The active object normally becomes the subject of the passive sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to the active subject in passive voice?

options.A: It becomes the subject of the passive sentence
options.B: It becomes the agent, usually introduced by 'by'

questions.explanation: The active subject becomes the agent, usually introduced by 'by'. It may be omitted if unknown, obvious or unimportant.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the past participle?

options.A: The first form (V1) of a verb
options.B: The second form (V2) of a verb
options.C: The third form (V3) of a verb

questions.explanation: The past participle is the third form (V3) of a verb: write-wrote-written; eat-ate-eaten; make-made-made.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does passive voice always require 'by'?

options.B: No, the agent can be omitted

questions.explanation: No. The agent can be omitted: 'The road was repaired.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'by + agent' omitted in passive voice?

options.A: When the agent is unknown, obvious, unimportant, general, or deliberately not stated
options.B: Only when the agent is a pronoun

questions.explanation: The agent is omitted when unknown, obvious, unimportant, general, or deliberately not stated: 'My wallet was stolen'; 'English is spoken here.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can every active sentence be changed into passive voice?

options.A: Yes, every sentence can be changed
options.B: No, only verbs that take an object (transitive verbs) normally form a personal passive
options.C: Only sentences in past tense can be changed
options.D: Only sentences with 'by' can be changed

questions.explanation: No. Only transitive verbs normally form a personal passive. Intransitive verbs such as sleep, arrive and happen do not normally have a passive form.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a transitive verb?

options.A: A verb that does not take a direct object
options.B: A verb that takes a direct object
options.C: A verb that links subject to complement

questions.explanation: A transitive verb takes a direct object: 'She wrote a letter.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an intransitive verb?

options.A: A verb that takes a direct object
options.B: A verb that does not take a direct object
options.C: A verb that takes two objects
options.D: A verb that takes an infinitive

questions.explanation: An intransitive verb does not take a direct object: 'The baby slept'; 'The train arrived.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why is 'He sleeps' not normally changed into passive voice?

options.B: Because 'sleep' is intransitive and has no direct object to become the passive subject
options.D: Because the sentence is a question

questions.explanation: Sleep is intransitive in this use and has no direct object to become the passive subject.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between active and passive voice in emphasis?

options.A: Active emphasises the receiver; passive emphasises the doer
options.B: Active usually emphasises the doer; passive often emphasises the action, receiver or result

questions.explanation: Active voice usually emphasises the doer; passive voice often emphasises the action, receiver or result.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the first step in changing active voice into passive voice?

options.A: Change the verb to past participle
options.B: Identify the subject, verb and object; check that the verb is transitive and the object can become the passive subject
options.D: Change the tense of the sentence

questions.explanation: The first step is to identify the subject, verb and object, check that the verb is transitive and that the object can become the passive subject.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to the active object during conversion?

options.B: It becomes the subject of the passive sentence

questions.explanation: The active object becomes the subject of the passive sentence: 'They built a bridge' → 'A bridge was built...'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is the active verb changed in passive voice?

options.A: Into the appropriate tense/aspect form of 'be' + V3

questions.explanation: The active verb is changed into the appropriate tense/aspect form of be + V3: 'writes' → 'is written'; 'wrote' → 'was written.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the object pronoun form of 'I' after 'by' in passive voice?
questions.explanation: I → me; he → him; she → her; we → us; they → them.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the object pronoun form of 'they' after 'by' in passive voice?
questions.explanation: They → them in object form after 'by'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to tense during conversion to passive voice?

options.B: Tense and time meaning must remain unchanged; only the grammatical structure changes

questions.explanation: The tense and time meaning must remain unchanged. Only the grammatical structure changes.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to singular and plural agreement in passive voice?

options.A: The passive verb agrees with the new subject
options.B: The passive verb always takes singular form
options.C: The passive verb always takes plural form

questions.explanation: The passive verb agrees with the new subject: 'A letter is written'; 'Letters are written.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Should every active sentence be converted mechanically?

options.A: Yes, mechanical conversion is always correct
options.B: No, the converted sentence must be grammatical, natural and preserve the original meaning
options.C: Yes, if the verb is transitive
options.D: No, only questions should be converted

questions.explanation: No. The converted sentence must be grammatical, natural and preserve the original meaning. Some verbs or sentence types do not allow a normal passive transformation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the usual conversion formula for passive voice?
questions.explanation: Passive: O + be (correct tense) + V3 + (by + S).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'She writes a letter' (simple present)?

options.A: A letter was written by her
options.B: A letter is written by her
options.C: A letter has been written by her
options.D: A letter is being written by her

questions.explanation: Simple present passive: am/is/are + V3. 'She writes a letter' → 'A letter is written by her.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'She is writing a letter' (present continuous)?

options.A: A letter is written by her
options.B: A letter is being written by her
options.C: A letter has been written by her
options.D: A letter was being written by her

questions.explanation: Present continuous passive: am/is/are + being + V3. 'She is writing a letter' → 'A letter is being written by her.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'She has written a letter' (present perfect)?

options.A: A letter is written by her
options.B: A letter has been written by her
options.C: A letter was written by her
options.D: A letter had been written by her

questions.explanation: Present perfect passive: has/have + been + V3. 'She has written a letter' → 'A letter has been written by her.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does present perfect continuous normally have a standard passive form in ordinary exam transformations?

options.B: No, normally no standard passive form is used

questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous ('She has been writing a letter') normally has no standard passive form used in ordinary exam transformations.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'She wrote a letter' (simple past)?

options.A: A letter is written by her
options.B: A letter was written by her
options.C: A letter has been written by her
options.D: A letter had been written by her

questions.explanation: Simple past passive: was/were + V3. 'She wrote a letter' → 'A letter was written by her.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'She was writing a letter' (past continuous)?

options.A: A letter was written by her
options.B: A letter was being written by her
options.C: A letter had been written by her
options.D: A letter is being written by her

questions.explanation: Past continuous passive: was/were + being + V3. 'She was writing a letter' → 'A letter was being written by her.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'She had written a letter' (past perfect)?

options.A: A letter was written by her
options.B: A letter had been written by her
options.C: A letter has been written by her
options.D: A letter will have been written by her

questions.explanation: Past perfect passive: had + been + V3. 'She had written a letter' → 'A letter had been written by her.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does past perfect continuous normally have a standard passive form in ordinary exam transformations?

options.B: No, normally no standard passive form is used

questions.explanation: Past perfect continuous ('She had been writing a letter') normally has no standard passive form used in ordinary exam transformations.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'She will write a letter' (simple future)?

options.A: A letter is written by her
options.B: A letter will be written by her
options.C: A letter will have been written by her
options.D: A letter would be written by her

questions.explanation: Simple future passive: will + be + V3. 'She will write a letter' → 'A letter will be written by her.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does future continuous normally have a standard passive form in ordinary exam transformations?

options.B: No, normally no standard passive form is used

questions.explanation: Future continuous ('She will be writing a letter') normally has no standard passive form used in ordinary exam transformations.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'She will have written a letter' (future perfect)?

options.A: A letter will be written by her
options.B: A letter will have been written by her
options.C: A letter has been written by her
options.D: A letter would have been written by her

questions.explanation: Future perfect passive: will + have + been + V3. 'She will have written a letter' → 'A letter will have been written by her.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does future perfect continuous normally have a standard passive form in ordinary exam transformations?

options.B: No, normally no standard passive form is used

questions.explanation: Future perfect continuous ('She will have been writing a letter') normally has no standard passive form used in ordinary exam transformations.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure of the simple present tense?
questions.explanation: Simple present passive: am/is/are + V3. Example: 'They clean the rooms' → 'The rooms are cleaned.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure of the present continuous tense?
questions.explanation: Present continuous passive: am/is/are + being + V3. Example: 'They are repairing the road' → 'The road is being repaired.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure of the present perfect tense?
questions.explanation: Present perfect passive: has/have + been + V3. Example: 'She has completed the work' → 'The work has been completed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure of the simple past tense?
questions.explanation: Simple past passive: was/were + V3. Example: 'The boy broke the glass' → 'The glass was broken.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure of the past continuous tense?
questions.explanation: Past continuous passive: was/were + being + V3. Example: 'They were painting the house' → 'The house was being painted.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure of the past perfect tense?
questions.explanation: Past perfect passive: had + been + V3. Example: 'He had sent the parcel' → 'The parcel had been sent.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure of the simple future tense?
questions.explanation: Simple future passive: will + be + V3. Example: 'They will announce the result' → 'The result will be announced.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure of the future perfect tense?
questions.explanation: Future perfect passive: will + have + been + V3. Example: 'She will have finished the work' → 'The work will have been finished.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why is 'being' used in continuous passive forms?

options.B: Being marks the progressive aspect: 'is being repaired', 'was being repaired'
options.C: Being is the past participle of be
options.D: Being is used only in future tense

questions.explanation: Being marks the progressive aspect: 'is being repaired,' 'was being repaired.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why is 'been' used in perfect passive forms?

options.B: Been is the past participle of be and combines with the perfect auxiliary: 'has been completed', 'had been written'
options.C: Been is the base form of be
options.D: Been is used only in simple past

questions.explanation: Been is the past participle of be and combines with the perfect auxiliary: 'has been completed,' 'had been written.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with 'can'?
questions.explanation: Modal passive: can + be + V3. 'They can solve the problem' → 'The problem can be solved.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with 'could'?
questions.explanation: Modal passive: could + be + V3. 'She could answer the question' → 'The question could be answered.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with 'may'?
questions.explanation: Modal passive: may + be + V3. 'They may postpone the meeting' → 'The meeting may be postponed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with 'might'?
questions.explanation: Modal passive: might + be + V3. 'He might cancel the trip' → 'The trip might be cancelled.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with 'must'?
questions.explanation: Modal passive: must + be + V3. 'You must obey the rules' → 'The rules must be obeyed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with 'should'?
questions.explanation: Modal passive: should + be + V3. 'We should respect elders' → 'Elders should be respected.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with 'ought to'?
questions.explanation: Modal passive: ought to + be + V3. 'You ought to complete the task' → 'The task ought to be completed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with 'have to/has to'?
questions.explanation: Passive: have to/has to + be + V3. 'They have to submit the form' → 'The form has to be submitted.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with 'had to'?
questions.explanation: Passive: had to + be + V3. 'They had to cancel the match' → 'The match had to be cancelled.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive structure with modal perfect?
questions.explanation: Modal perfect passive: modal + have + been + V3. 'They may have stolen the car' → 'The car may have been stolen.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'need to' changed into passive?
questions.explanation: Need to + be + V3. 'You need to complete the application' → 'The application needs to be completed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a negative active sentence changed into passive?

options.B: Keep the negative meaning and place 'not' after the first auxiliary
options.D: Place 'not' at the end of the sentence

questions.explanation: Keep the negative meaning and place not after the first auxiliary: 'They did not invite him' → 'He was not invited.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a yes/no question changed into passive?

options.B: Retain the question form and move the correct auxiliary before the new subject
options.D: Change the question into a statement

questions.explanation: Retain the question form and move the correct auxiliary before the new subject: 'Did she write the letter?' → 'Was the letter written by her?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'Do they sell cars?'

options.B: Do cars be sold by them?

questions.explanation: Present simple question passive: 'Do they sell cars?' → 'Are cars sold by them?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'Has he completed the work?'

options.A: Has the work been completed by him?
options.B: Has the work completed by him?
options.C: Was the work completed by him?
options.D: Is the work completed by him?

questions.explanation: Present perfect question passive: 'Has he completed the work?' → 'Has the work been completed by him?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'Can you solve this?'

options.A: Can this be solved by you?
options.C: This can be solved by you?
options.D: Could this be solved by you?

questions.explanation: Modal question passive: 'Can you solve this?' → 'Can this be solved by you?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a wh- question changed into passive?

options.B: Retain the question word: 'Why did they arrest him?' → 'Why was he arrested?'

questions.explanation: Retain the question word: 'Why did they arrest him?' → 'Why was he arrested?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a question beginning with 'who' changed into formal passive?

options.B: Use 'By whom was...': 'Who wrote this poem?' → 'By whom was this poem written?'

questions.explanation: If 'who' is the active subject, use 'by whom' in a formal passive: 'Who wrote this poem?' → 'By whom was this poem written?' A natural alternative is 'Who was this poem written by?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a question beginning with 'whom' changed into passive?

options.A: Whom as active object can become the passive subject: 'Whom did they select?' → 'Who was selected by them?'

questions.explanation: Whom as an active object can become the passive subject: 'Whom did they select?' → 'Who was selected by them?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a negative modal sentence changed into passive?

options.B: Keep 'not' after the modal: 'You must not break the rules' → 'The rules must not be broken.'

questions.explanation: Keep not after the modal: 'You must not break the rules' → 'The rules must not be broken.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an imperative sentence?

options.A: A sentence that asks a question
options.B: A sentence that expresses a command, request, instruction, advice or prohibition
options.C: A sentence that states a fact
options.D: A sentence that expresses a wish

questions.explanation: An imperative sentence expresses a command, request, instruction, advice or prohibition: 'Close the door'; 'Please help me.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a command commonly changed into passive?
questions.explanation: Use 'Let + object + be + V3': 'Open the door' → 'Let the door be opened.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a negative command changed into passive?
questions.explanation: Use 'Let + object + not + be + V3': 'Do not touch the switch' → 'Let the switch not be touched.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How can a request be changed into passive?

options.A: Use 'You are requested/asked to + base verb' where appropriate: 'Please help me' → 'You are requested to help me.'

questions.explanation: Use 'You are requested/asked to + base verb' where appropriate: 'Please help me' → 'You are requested to help me.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How can advice be changed into passive?

options.A: Use an appropriate passive expression: 'Follow the rules' → 'You are advised to follow the rules' or 'The rules should be followed.'

questions.explanation: Use an appropriate passive expression: 'Follow the rules' → 'You are advised to follow the rules' or 'The rules should be followed,' depending on the intended meaning.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is 'Let the door be opened' the only possible passive form of a command?

options.A: Yes, it is the only form
options.B: No, the suitable passive depends on the function and context; 'The door should be opened' or 'You are requested to open the door' may be more natural
options.D: No, only 'The door should be opened' is correct

questions.explanation: No. The suitable passive depends on the function and context; 'The door should be opened' or 'You are requested to open the door' may be more natural.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a ditransitive verb?

options.A: A verb that takes no object
options.B: A verb that can take both an indirect object and a direct object
options.C: A verb that takes only a direct object
options.D: A verb that links subject to complement

questions.explanation: A ditransitive verb can take both an indirect object and a direct object: give, send, teach, offer, show, tell.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a sentence with two objects have two passive forms?

options.A: No, only one passive form is possible
options.B: Often yes, because either object may become the passive subject
options.C: Yes, but only in past tense
options.D: No, two-object verbs cannot be made passive

questions.explanation: Often yes, because either object may become the passive subject: 'She gave me a book' → 'I was given a book' or 'A book was given to me.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the passive forms of 'They sent him a letter'?

options.A: He was sent a letter / A letter was sent to him
options.B: He is sent a letter / A letter is sent to him
options.C: He was sent a letter / A letter was sent him
options.D: Him was sent a letter / A letter was sent to he

questions.explanation: 'They sent him a letter' → 'He was sent a letter' or 'A letter was sent to him.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the passive forms of 'The teacher taught us grammar'?

options.A: We were taught grammar / Grammar was taught to us
options.B: Us were taught grammar / Grammar was taught to we
options.C: We are taught grammar / Grammar is taught to us
options.D: We had been taught grammar / Grammar had been taught to us

questions.explanation: 'The teacher taught us grammar' → 'We were taught grammar' or 'Grammar was taught to us.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can every indirect object become a passive subject?

options.B: No, the possibility depends on the verb and its construction; some verbs allow only one natural passive form

questions.explanation: No. The possibility depends on the verb and its construction. Some verbs allow only one natural passive form.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is an infinitive object changed in passive?

options.B: Use 'to be + V3': 'They want someone to repair the car' → 'They want the car to be repaired.'

questions.explanation: Use 'to be + V3': 'They want someone to repair the car' → 'They want the car to be repaired.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a gerund object changed in passive?

options.B: Use 'being + V3': 'I dislike people interrupting me' → 'I dislike being interrupted.'

questions.explanation: Use 'being + V3': 'I dislike people interrupting me' → 'I dislike being interrupted.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a verb followed by an infinitive changed into passive?

options.A: The passive infinitive is 'to be + V3': 'They expect him to win' → 'He is expected to win.'

questions.explanation: The passive infinitive is 'to be + V3': 'They expect him to win' → 'He is expected to win.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a reporting verb used in passive?

options.A: Use 'It is said/believed/thought that...' or subject + passive reporting verb + to-infinitive

questions.explanation: With verbs such as say, believe, think, know, report and expect, use 'It is said/believed/thought that...' or subject + passive reporting verb + to-infinitive.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the passive forms of 'People say that he is honest'?

options.A: It is said that he is honest / He is said to be honest
options.B: He is said that he is honest
options.C: It is said to be honest

questions.explanation: 'People say that he is honest' → 'It is said that he is honest' or 'He is said to be honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the passive forms of 'People believe that she stole the money'?

options.A: It is believed that she stole the money / She is believed to have stolen the money
options.B: She is believed that she stole the money
options.C: It is believed to steal the money
options.D: She believed to have stolen the money

questions.explanation: 'People believe that she stole the money' → 'It is believed that she stole the money' or 'She is believed to have stolen the money.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'They expect him to arrive'?

options.C: It is expected him to arrive
options.D: He is expected to be arrived

questions.explanation: 'They expect him to arrive' → 'He is expected to arrive.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a prepositional verb changed into passive?

options.B: Keep the required preposition: 'They laughed at him' → 'He was laughed at.'

questions.explanation: Keep the required preposition: 'They laughed at him' → 'He was laughed at.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'They looked after the child'?
questions.explanation: 'They looked after the child' → 'The child was looked after.' The preposition/particle after remains.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the passive form of 'Someone has broken into the house'?

options.A: The house has been broken into

questions.explanation: 'Someone has broken into the house' → 'The house has been broken into.' Keep the preposition into.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are verbs such as give, make and elect used in passive complements?

options.B: The object complement remains after the passive verb: 'They elected him president' → 'He was elected president.'
options.C: The object complement becomes the subject
options.D: The object complement becomes the agent

questions.explanation: The object complement remains after the passive verb: 'They elected him president' → 'He was elected president.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is an object complement retained in passive?

options.B: It remains after the passive verb: 'They painted the wall blue' → 'The wall was painted blue.'

questions.explanation: The object complement remains after the passive verb: 'They painted the wall blue' → 'The wall was painted blue.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a passive sentence have no by-agent?

options.B: Yes: 'The documents have been signed'; the agent is not stated

questions.explanation: Yes: 'The documents have been signed'; the agent is not stated.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is get-passive used?

options.A: Get + V3 can express an event or change, often informal: 'He got injured.' It is not suitable as a replacement in every passive sentence.

questions.explanation: Get + V3 can express an event or change, often informal: 'He got injured.' It is not suitable as a replacement in every passive sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Verbs That Do Not Normally Form Passive
questions.question: Which verbs generally cannot be changed into passive voice?

options.B: Intransitive verbs without an object: sleep, arrive, come, go, happen, occur, die, fall, rise, exist

questions.explanation: Intransitive verbs without an object generally cannot be changed into passive voice: sleep, arrive, come, go, happen, occur, die, fall, rise, exist.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Verbs That Do Not Normally Form Passive
questions.question: Why can 'The baby slept' not be made passive?

options.B: Because 'slept' has no direct object to become the passive subject
options.D: Because the sentence is a question

questions.explanation: Slept has no direct object to become the passive subject.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Verbs That Do Not Normally Form Passive
questions.question: Can 'The accident happened' be changed into passive?

options.B: No, 'happen' is intransitive in this use and does not take a direct object

questions.explanation: No. Happen is intransitive in this use and does not take a direct object.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Verbs That Do Not Normally Form Passive
questions.question: Can linking verbs normally be changed into passive?
